fetched_contents.text: Does Foreign-Accented Speech Affect Credibility? Evidence from the Illusory-Truth Paradigm Abstract In a pioneering study, Lev-Ari and Keysar (2010) observed that unknown statements are judged less credible when uttered with foreign accent compared to native accent. This finding was interpreted in terms of processing fluency; when intelligibility is reduced, the credibility of the message decreases. Here, we use the illusory truth paradigm to explore how accent affects credibility. In a between-participant design, participants were exposed to unknown statements uttered by native-accented or foreign-accented speakers. After a distractor task, the same statements were presented with new statements, and participants assessed their truthfulness. Truthfulness ratings were higher for repeated statements than for new statements, replicating the illusory truth effect. Contrary to the processing fluency hypothesis, the effect was similar in both the foreign-accented and native-accented speech groups. A new group of participants rated the speakers’ voices on various social traits. A negative bias against foreign speakers was observed. However, this negative-bias did not affect truth ratings.The impact of foreign-accented speech on message credibility is discussed in the context of two factors, processing fluency and out-group stereotype activation. Keywords: Foreign-accented speech, Credibility, Fluency processing, Illusory-truth effect, Intelligibility, Foreignness, Out-group stereotype Introduction Several characteristics of the speech signal may determine how listeners interpret a spoken message. For instance, indexical properties of the voice, such as pitch or volume, can influence the way a sentence like “I have a large tattoo on my back” is interpreted, depending on whether the voice is associated with a child or an adult (Van Berkum et al., 2008). Another characteristic of speech is the accent, which is defined as the idiosyncratic way in which each speaker pronounces words and sentences of a language. A topic that has received significant attention in the cognitive and social sciences is whether the accent used to convey a spoken message affects its interpretation. Here, we explore whether accent modulates message credibility by contrasting foreign-accented and native-accented speech. The accent of a speaker is shaped by their linguistic and cultural heritage. Listeners naturally and effortlessly draw upon this information, forming distinct personal impressions of speakers based on their accent (Cargile & Giles, 1997; Cargile et al., 1994; Ryan, 1983). It has been suggested that a negative bias exists in adult listeners, as they typically judge speakers with a foreign-accent as less trustworthy, less educated, less intelligent, and less competent than native-accented speakers (Dewaele & McCloskey, 2015; Fraser & Kelly, 2012; Fuertes et al., 2012; Giles & Watson, 2013; Gluszek & Dovidio, 2010). This negative bias may have two origins (Foucart et al., 2020). One origin is socially-driven and initiates with the automatic categorization of a foreign-accented speaker as an out-group individual (Baus et al., 2017; Baus et al., 2021; Champoux-Larsson et al., 2022; Kinzler, Dupoux & Spelke, 2010; Pietraszewski & Schwartz, 2014a; Lorenzoni et al., 2022a). The sensitivity toward accents is evident from childhood (Kinzler et al., 2007) and it remains stable in adulthood (Pietraszewski & Schwartz, 2014b). Importantly, the automatic categorization linked to foreign accents seems to trigger stereotypes and stigmas associated with the respective foreign groups (Ryan, 1983; Wated & Sanchez, 2006). The activation of these stereotypes may affect the trustworthiness of the message, influencing message credibility (Giles & Watson 2013; Ryan, 1983; Stevenage, Clarke & McNeill, 2012). A second origin of the negative bias refers to the fact that foreign-accented speech deviates from the standard pronunciation of the listener. Consequently, foreign-accented speech is often perceived as less fluent than native-accented speech and can be more challenging to understand. Several studies support the claim that processing difficulty is inversely related to the truth-value assigned to the message (i.e., the processing fluency hypothesis, Oppenheimer, 2008). Cognitive fluency refers to the ease and speed with which people process information, and it is related to the concept of mental (cognitive) effort required to complete a task. The amount of mental effort involved in solving a task determines not only the outcome but also how people perceive the information regarding the task. Those tasks that require less mental effort can lead to greater confidence during task resolution and a more positive overall experience. That is, the information that is presented under these circumstances is easy to process and understand and, at the same time, it tends to be perceived as more familiar and trustworthy (e.g., Oppenheimer, 2008). Contrarily, under circumstances of more cognitive mental effort, information is more difficult to process and understand. This information is perceived as unfamiliar and untrustworthy, leading to a negative experience. In a pioneering study, Reber and Schwarz (1999) manipulated the colour font of several statements and the background colour of the screen on which they were presented. In doing so, some statements were easier to read than others. Statements were judged as truer when they were presented in easier-to-read colour contrasts. In relation to spoken language, foreign-accented speech diverges from standard (native) speech; therefore, it is perceived as less fluent. The inherent difficulty in processing foreign accent may negatively affect the credibility of the message (Dragojevic et al., 2017; Schwarz, 2004; Formanowicz & Suitner, 2020). What phonemic differences in European-accented English affect American listeners

The evidence here suggests that phonemic differences in European-accented English are noticeable and can influence American listeners, but the provided search material is thin on specific European-English phonemic contrasts. The strongest direct phonemic evidence comes from a search excerpt indicating that American-English vowel perception by Spanish-English bilinguals has focused on contrasts such as /i/-/Éª/ (e.g., sheep/ship) [N1-R1]. Another excerpt notes that accent perception by L2 speakers contrasts European English with the American English accent as the “de facto standard” in English-language education [N1-R2]. A third excerpt says that the strength of a speaker’s accent significantly affected listeners’ comprehensibility ratings, and most speakers were highly intelligible, with transcription evidence [N1-R3]. Finally, a search excerpt says that listeners from diverse language backgrounds weighed phonetic parameters such as segmental features including consonants and vowels [N1-R4].

From this, the most defensible conclusion is that phonemic differences relevant to American listeners include vowel contrasts, consonants, and intelligibility-related segmental features, but the evidence does not identify a complete set of European-specific phonemic contrasts. The European-accented English material in the search results is more general than specific; it points to accent as a phonetic category that differs from the American standard and can affect comprehension and perceived intelligibility [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4].

As for which phonemes are most noticeable or judgment-relevant, the evidence is not precise enough to name a full list. The strongest relevant claim is that phonetic parameters such as segmental features are weighted in listener judgments [N1-R4]. The intelligibility excerpt also suggests that accent strength correlates with comprehensibility, which implies that listeners attend to phonemic features that make speech easier or harder to understand [N1-R3]. However, the provided material does not isolate a single European-English phoneme as especially judgment-relevant.

On the question of how phonemic differences correlate with perceived fluency or comprehension, the evidence is more explicit. The excerpt on accent strength says that stronger accents significantly affected listeners’ comprehensibility ratings [N1-R3]. Another excerpt says that accent perception by L2 speakers contrasts European English with the American standard [N1-R2], implying that phonemic differences from the standard can create a perception of non-standardness, which is related to fluency. The search excerpt on phonetic parameters also says listeners weigh segmental features such as consonants and vowels [N1-R4]. Overall, the evidence supports the idea that phonemic differences contribute to perceived fluency and comprehension, especially when accent strength is high and intelligibility is reduced [N1-R3][N1-R4].

Because the search material does not provide detailed phonemic contrasts specific to European-accented English, this aggregate is best characterized as evidence-based but limited in specificity. The strongest supported points are that segmental features matter, accent strength affects comprehensibility, and European-accented English is contrasted with the American standard [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4].

What prosodic differences in European-accented English affect American listeners

The evidence here is stronger on prosody than on phonemic differences. The provided search material explicitly connects prosody to speech perception and evaluation. One excerpt says that accent perception studies examine suprasegmental characteristics of nonnative speakers, combining indices of speech rate, pause, and other suprasegmental features [N4-R3]. Another excerpt says that studies investigate the relative contribution of L2 intonation, rhythm, and speech rate to L1 perceptions of accentedness and comprehensibility [N2-R2]. A third excerpt notes that an additional aim was to examine the role of prosodic elements in L2 listeners’ speech perception in noise and how this is handled [N2-R3]. A methodological review also states that accents are defined as a “loose bundle of prosodic and segmental features” [N4-F3].

From these sources, the key prosodic patterns that differ in European-accented English are likely intonation, rhythm, speech rate, pause, and possibly other suprasegmental features. The evidence does not isolate a single European-specific prosodic contrast, but it does establish that prosodic variation is a major area of study in accent perception [N2-R2][N2-R3][N4-R3]. The methodological review also emphasizes that accents include prosody and segmental features, and that accent is distributed over geographic and social space [N4-F3]. That framing supports the idea that prosodic differences are part of the broader “accent” that listeners perceive.

How prosody relates to perceived naturalness, effort, or authority is supported by the evidence. The methodological review says that accent is a socially significant marker and that listeners use it to infer identity traits such as intelligence, socio-economic background, and friendliness [N4-F3]. It also says that a negative bias against foreign speakers is observed, and that the negative bias may have two origins: automatic categorization and stereotype activation [N5-F2]. This implies that prosodic cues can contribute to perceptions of effort and authority because they shape how listeners categorize and stereotype speakers. The search excerpt on accent perception by L2 speakers also suggests that accent is contrasted with the American standard, which is the de facto standard in language education [N1-R2], reinforcing the idea that prosodic differences can signal deviation from a standard model and thus affect naturalness judgments.

On whether prosodic cues are more reliable than phonemic cues in evaluation, the evidence does not directly compare reliability across cue types. However, the methodological review explicitly says that accents are a “loose bundle of prosodic and segmental features” [N4-F3], implying that both types of features are important. The accent perception excerpt also says that listeners weigh segmental features such as consonants and vowels [N1-R4], while the suprasegmental excerpt says studies examine suprasegmental characteristics [N4-R3]. Together, these suggest that both phonemic and prosodic cues are used, but the provided evidence does not establish which is more reliable overall. The closest conclusion is that prosodic cues are central to evaluation, especially for accentedness and comprehensibility, but the evidence does not support a definitive ranking of prosodic vs phonemic reliability [N4-R3][N4-F3][N1-R4].

Overall, the evidence supports a picture in which European-accented English differs prosodically in intonation, rhythm, speech rate, pause, and other suprasegmental features, and these differences can affect perceived naturalness, effort, and stereotype-linked attitudes. The evidence is strongest on the existence of prosodic variation and its relevance to perception, but thinner on specific European-English contrasts or a direct comparison of prosodic vs phonemic reliability [N2-R2][N2-R3][N4-R3][N4-F3].

How American listeners evaluate speakers with European accents

The evidence here shows that American listeners evaluate speakers with European accents along several dimensions, but the provided search material is more general than specific to European accents alone. The strongest direct support is that accent strength significantly affects listeners’ comprehensibility ratings [N1-R3]. Another excerpt says that listeners from diverse language backgrounds weighed phonetic parameters such as segmental features [N1-R4]. The methodological review notes that accents are defined as a “loose bundle of prosodic and segmental features” and that they are socially significant markers used to infer identity traits such as intelligence, socio-economic background, race, region of origin, friendliness, etc. [N4-F3]. It also notes that research has shown a negative bias against foreign speakers, including negative evaluations of intelligence, friendliness, and competence [N5-F2]. A separate excerpt says that foreign-accented speech can be judged more negatively than native-accented speech, and that heavy accents are evaluated more negatively than mild accents [N5-F1].

From this, the main evaluative dimensions are fluency/fluency-related processing, comprehensibility, and attitude/social evaluation. The evidence on fluency is especially strong: accent strength disrupts processing fluency, and stronger accents are judged less favorably [N1-R3][N5-F1]. The evidence on attitude/social evaluation is also strong: listeners associate accents with identity traits and negative stereotypes, and foreign accents are often judged less trustworthy, less educated, less intelligent, and less competent than native accents [N4-F3][N5-F2]. The evidence on comprehensibility is also present: accent strength significantly affects comprehensibility ratings [N1-R3].

Whether European accents are judged more positively or negatively overall is not directly answered by the provided evidence. However, the evidence does support a general negative bias against foreign accents, including strong accents being judged more negatively than mild accents [N5-F1][N5-F2]. It also says that the negative bias may have two origins: automatic categorization and stereotype activation [N5-F2]. This suggests that European accents, like other foreign accents, can be judged negatively, but the evidence does not establish that all European accents are uniformly negative or that any European accent is consistently judged more positively than others. The provided material does not isolate European accents from other foreign accents, so a stronger conclusion would be that European accents may be judged negatively when accent strength is high and stereotype-negative associations are activated [N5-F1][N5-F2].

The evidence on listener demographics or exposure is mixed but present. The methodological review says that research has shown a negative bias against foreign speakers and that accent is shaped by linguistic and cultural heritage [N4-F3][N5-F2]. The search excerpt on accent perception by L2 speakers notes that listeners from diverse language backgrounds weigh phonetic parameters [N1-R4]. The evidence also suggests that listener familiarity with an accent and language experience affect recognition [N6-R1][N6-R4]. However, the provided material does not give specific findings on whether American listeners differ by age, education, exposure to European speech, or other demographics in a way that is directly tied to European accents. It does, however, support the broader idea that listener exposure and familiarity with accents can shape evaluations [N6-R1][N6-R4].

Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that American listeners evaluate speakers with European accents primarily through fluency, comprehensibility, and attitude/social evaluation. The evidence is strongest that stronger accents are judged less favorably, and that accents can trigger negative stereotypes and bias against foreign speakers [N1-R3][N5-F1][N5-F2]. The evidence is thinner on whether European accents are consistently more positive or negative overall, and thinner still on specific demographic effects [N5-F2][N6-R1][N6-R4].
